04.01.title: Error analysis and convergence order
04.01.html:
Every numerical method trades effort for accuracy. The question an engineer asks is not “is it accurate?” but “how fast does the error fall when I pay more?” That rate, the order of convergence, is the single most useful number for comparing methods, choosing step sizes and catching bugs. A solver that should be second order but measures as first order has a mistake in it, every time.

Two kinds of convergence

Iterative methods (root finders, linear solvers) produce a sequence x0​,x1​,… with error en​=∣xn​−x∗∣. The method has order p if

en+1​≈Cenp​.

p=1 is linear (each step multiplies the error by C<1), p=2 is quadratic (the number of correct digits roughly doubles per step).

Discretisation methods (finite differences, quadrature, ODE solvers) have a step h and error

E(h)≈Khp.

Halving h divides the error by 2p: by 4 for a second-order method, by 16 for a fourth-order one.

Measuring the order from data

Take logs and the power law becomes a straight line. For an iteration, three consecutive errors give

p≈ln(en​/en−1​)ln(en+1​/en​)​.

For a discretisation, two step sizes give p≈ln(E1​/E2​)/ln(h1​/h2​); with more points, fit a line to logE against logh. When the exact answer is unknown, compare three solutions at h, h/2, h/4: p≈log2​((uh​−uh/2​)/(uh/2​−uh/4​)).

Truncation versus round-off

Shrinking h reduces the truncation error Khp, but every function value carries a relative rounding error near ε≈2.2×10−16, and a difference formula divides it by h. The total error behaves like

E(h)≈Khp+hε∣f∣​,

so there is a best step. For the forward difference (p=1) it’s near ε​≈10−8; for the central difference (p=2) near ε1/3≈6×10−6. Below that, the error grows again.

Worked exampleNewton’s order, measured

Solve Wallis’s cubic x3−2x−5=0 (root x∗=2.0945515) with Newton’s method from x0​=3.

  1. Errors: 0.91, 0.27, 3.3×10−2, 5.8×10−4, 1.9×10−7, 2.1×10−14.
  2. Last triple: p≈ln(2.1×10−14/1.9×10−7)/ln(1.9×10−7/5.8×10−4)=2.00.
  3. Theory predicts C=∣f′′(x∗)/(2f′(x∗))∣=6x∗/(2(3x∗2−2))=0.563. Check: 2.1×10−14/(1.9×10−7)2≈0.58.
  4. The secant method on the same equation measures p≈1.61, close to the golden ratio 1.618 that theory predicts.

Exercise 1Read the order off a table

A solver for a beam deflection returns u=4.2860 mm at h=0.1 m, 4.2884 mm at h=0.05 m and 4.2890 mm at h=0.025 m. What order does it show, and what is the extrapolated answer?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Differences: 4.2884−4.2860=0.0024 and 4.2890−4.2884=0.0006.
  2. Ratio 0.0024/0.0006=4, so p=log2​4=2: second order.
  3. Richardson extrapolation: u≈uh/4​+(uh/4​−uh/2​)/(2p−1)=4.2890+0.0006/3=4.2892 mm.

04.02.title: Root finding toolbox
04.02.html:
Engineering is full of equations you cannot rearrange: the Colebrook friction factor in a pipe, the natural frequencies of a beam, the operating point of a pump on a system curve. You met bisection and Newton in Phase 01. This lesson builds the toolbox a professional uses: know which method is safe, which is fast, and how to combine them so you get both.

The trade-off

Method Needs Order Can fail?
Bisection a bracket [a,b] with a sign change 1 (halves the bracket) no
Newton f′ and a good start 2 yes: diverges, cycles, f′=0
Secant two starting points 1.618 yes
Brent a bracket superlinear no

Bisection is guaranteed but slow: to shrink a bracket of width L to δ takes ⌈log2​(L/δ)⌉ steps, independent of the function. Newton is fast but needs a derivative and can be thrown far away by a flat region.

Secant: Newton without the derivative

Replace f′(xn​) by the slope through the last two points:

xn+1​=xn​−f(xn​)f(xn​)−f(xn−1​)xn​−xn−1​​.

One new function evaluation per step and order φ=1.618. Per evaluation that beats Newton (which needs f and f′) whenever the derivative costs more than about 44% of a function call.

Brent: fast when it can be, safe when it must be

Brent’s method keeps a bracket at all times. Each step it tries a fast interpolation step: inverse quadratic interpolation through the last three points (fit x as a quadratic in y and set y=0), or a secant step. It accepts that step only if it lands inside the bracket and shrinks the interval well enough; otherwise it bisects. So it is never slower than bisection by more than a constant factor and usually converges superlinearly. It’s what scipy.optimize.brentq runs.

Worked exampleFriction factor in a water main

Find the Darcy friction factor f for Re=105 and relative roughness ε/D=10−4 from Colebrook:

f​1​=−2log10​(3.7ε/D​+Ref​2.51​).
  1. Solve for x=1/f​: g(x)=x+2log10​(ε/D/3.7+2.51x/Re)=0.
  2. Bracket: g(1)=−7.57 and g(20)=+13.45, so a root lies in [1,20].
  3. Brent converges in 6 iterations to x=7.3494, so f=1/x2=0.01851. Bisection needs 45 iterations for the same 10−12 tolerance.
  4. Sanity check against the explicit Swamee-Jain approximation: 0.01845, within 0.4%.

Exercise 1Choose the method

You need the first natural frequency of a clamped beam from cosβcoshβ=−1, inside a design loop that calls it 10 000 times. The derivative is easy. Which method do you use and how do you start it?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. The root near β=1.875 lies in the bracket [1,3]: cos1cosh1+1=1.83>0 and cos3cosh3+1=−8.97<0.
  2. Brent with that bracket is safe and fast. Newton is faster per step, but coshβ grows quickly, so a bad start can throw it to another root.
  3. A good compromise for the loop: Newton started from the previous design’s root, falling back to Brent if a step leaves the bracket. That is the same idea Brent uses internally.

04.03.title: Nonlinear systems
04.03.html:
Real structures rarely give you one equation in one unknown. A cable net, a linkage, a pipe network or a large-deflection frame gives you n coupled nonlinear equations F(x)=0. Newton’s method carries over almost unchanged: replace the derivative by the Jacobian matrix and the division by a linear solve. It is the engine inside every nonlinear finite-element code.

Newton in n dimensions

Linearise around the current guess:

F(x+Δx)≈F(x)+J(x)Δx,Jij​=∂xj​∂Fi​​.

Set the linear model to zero and solve for the step:

J(xk​)Δx=−F(xk​),xk+1​=xk​+Δx.

Never invert J; solve the system (LU from Phase 02). Near the solution the convergence is quadratic: the residual norm squares each step.

Where the Jacobian comes from

  • By hand, when the equations are simple. Best accuracy and speed.
  • By finite differences, column by column: J:,j​≈(F(x+hej​)−F(x−hej​))/(2h). Costs 2n residual evaluations. Always use it to check a hand-derived Jacobian.
  • By automatic differentiation, in modern frameworks.

A node held by two cables

A node at p hangs from elastic cables anchored at ai​ with unstretched length L0,i​ and axial stiffness EA. With di​=ai​−p, Li​=∣di​∣ and ui​=di​/Li​, each cable pulls with tension Ti​=L0,i​EA​(Li​−L0,i​) (zero if slack). Equilibrium is

F(p)=i∑​Ti​ui​+(0−W​)=0.

Differentiating gives the tangent stiffness, two physical parts per cable:

J=−i∑​[ki​ui​uiT​+Li​Ti​​(I−ui​uiT​)],ki​=L0,i​EA​.

The first term is the cable’s axial stiffness. The second is the geometric stiffness: a taut cable resists sideways motion in proportion to its tension, which is why a guitar string gets stiffer as you tune it up.

Worked exampleEquilibrium of the two-cable node

Anchors at (0,0) and (4,0) m, L0​=2.5 m and 2.0 m, EA=50 kN, W=2000 N, start at (2,−2) m.

  1. At the start both cables are 2.828 m long, so both are stretched; residual norm 2.0×104 N.
  2. Newton residuals: 2.0×104→2.9×103→2.6×102→3.2→6.4×10−4→2.7×10−11 N. Five steps, quadratic at the end.
  3. Solution p=(2.2991,−1.1971) m. Cable lengths 2.5921 m and 2.0799 m.
  4. Tensions T1​=50000⋅0.0921/2.5=1842 N and T2​=50000⋅0.0799/2.0=1997 N. Their vertical components add up to W.

04.04.title: Interpolation
04.04.html:
Measurements and tables give you values at a few points: a thermocouple calibration, a steam table, a cam profile, a wind-tunnel sweep. Interpolation fills in between. The obvious idea, one polynomial through all the points, works beautifully for a handful of points and fails spectacularly for many equally spaced ones. Understanding why tells you where to put your sample points.

Lagrange form

Through n+1 points (xj​,yj​) there is exactly one polynomial of degree at most n:

p(x)=j=0∑n​yj​ℓj​(x),ℓj​(x)=k=j∏​xj​−xk​x−xk​​.

Each basis polynomial ℓj​ is 1 at its own node and 0 at the others. For computing, use the barycentric form, which is stable and costs O(n) per evaluation:

p(x)=∑j​x−xj​wj​​∑j​x−xj​wj​​yj​​,wj​=∏k=j​(xj​−xk​)1​.

The error formula and Runge’s phenomenon

For a smooth f,

f(x)−p(x)=(n+1)!f(n+1)(ξ)​j=0∏n​(x−xj​).

Two factors fight: the derivative term and the node polynomial ∏(x−xj​). For equally spaced nodes the node polynomial is tiny in the middle and huge near the ends. For f=1/(1+25x2) on [−1,1], the derivatives grow fast enough that the error near the ends grows with n: Runge’s phenomenon.

Chebyshev nodes

Choose nodes that cluster towards the ends:

xk​=cos2(n+1)(2k+1)π​,k=0,…,n.

They make max∣∏(x−xk​)∣=2−n, the smallest possible, and for any smooth function the interpolation error then falls as n grows. When you can choose where to measure, measure at Chebyshev points.

Worked exampleThermocouple between table values

A type K thermocouple gives 0 mV at 0 °C, 4.096 mV at 100 °C and 8.138 mV at 200 °C. Estimate the voltage at 150 °C.

  1. ℓ0​(150)=(0−100)(0−200)(150−100)(150−200)​=−0.125.
  2. ℓ1​(150)=(100−0)(100−200)(150−0)(150−200)​=0.75, and ℓ2​(150)=200⋅100150⋅50​=0.375.
  3. p(150)=0+0.75⋅4.096+0.375⋅8.138=6.124 mV.
  4. The reference table gives 6.138 mV. The 0.014 mV gap is about 0.35 °C at roughly 41 µV/°C: fine for a quick check, not for calibration, where you’d use more points or a spline.

The script prints, for Runge’s function:

n equispaced max error Chebyshev max error
5 0.433 0.556
10 1.916 0.109
15 2.108 0.083
20 59.8 0.015

At very low degree Chebyshev is not automatically better, but only Chebyshev keeps improving.

Exercise 1Why not just use more points?

A colleague fits a degree-20 polynomial through 21 equally spaced points of a measured cam lift curve and finds wild oscillations near the ends. Give two fixes.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Measure at Chebyshev-spaced angles instead, if the rig allows it. The node polynomial is then evenly small across the interval.
  2. Use piecewise interpolation: a cubic spline (next lesson) through the same 21 points. Each piece only sees its neighbours, so the error is controlled locally and doesn’t grow with the number of points.
  3. If the data are noisy, don’t interpolate at all: fit a low-degree least-squares model (Phase 02) or a smoothing spline.

04.05.title: Splines
04.05.html:
A draughtsman bending a thin wooden strip through pins on a drawing board was solving a variational problem: the strip settles into the shape with the least bending energy. That shape, piecewise cubic with continuous slope and curvature, is the cubic spline. It’s how CAD tools draw smooth curves, how cam profiles are designed and how you interpolate measured data without Runge’s wiggles.

Conditions on each piece

Between knots xi​ and xi+1​ (spacing hi​) the spline is a cubic Si​(x). With n intervals there are 4n coefficients. Conditions:

  • Si​(xi​)=yi​ and Si​(xi+1​)=yi+1​: 2n conditions.
  • slope continuous at the n−1 interior knots.
  • second derivative (curvature) continuous at the interior knots.

That is 4n−2. The last two come from the ends: a natural spline sets S′′=0 at both ends (a free strip), a clamped spline prescribes the end slopes.

Solve for the curvatures

Use the knot second derivatives Mi​=S′′(xi​) as unknowns. Within an interval S′′ is linear, so integrating twice and imposing the values gives, with A=(xi+1​−x)/hi​ and B=1−A,

S(x)=Ayi​+Byi+1​+6hi2​​[(A3−A)Mi​+(B3−B)Mi+1​].

Slope continuity at each interior knot then becomes one equation linking three neighbours:

hi−1​Mi−1​+2(hi−1​+hi​)Mi​+hi​Mi+1​=6(hi​yi+1​−yi​​−hi−1​yi​−yi−1​​).

The matrix is tridiagonal and diagonally dominant, so the Thomas algorithm (Gaussian elimination without fill-in) solves it in O(n) operations. A million-knot spline costs milliseconds.

Worked exampleA four-knot natural spline by hand

Knots (0,0), (1,1), (2,0), (3,1), all h=1, natural ends M0​=M3​=0.

  1. Knot 1: M0​+4M1​+M2​=6(y0​−2y1​+y2​)=−12.
  2. Knot 2: M1​+4M2​+M3​=6(y1​−2y2​+y3​)=12.
  3. Solve 4M1​+M2​=−12, M1​+4M2​=12: M1​=−4, M2​=4.
  4. At x=0.5 (A=B=0.5): S=0.5⋅0+0.5⋅1+61​(−0.375⋅0−0.375⋅(−4))=0.5+0.25=0.75.

The continuity test is worth having: an early version of the code above built the sub-diagonal from the wrong spacings. With uneven knots the curve still passed through every point and looked fine, but the slope jumped at the third station. Only the test caught it.

Exercise 1Natural or clamped?

A cam profile must start from rest: lift 0 and slope 0 at θ=0. Which end condition do you use there, and what does a natural spline do instead?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Use a clamped end with S′(0)=0, so the follower velocity starts at zero.
  2. A natural spline forces S′′(0)=0 instead and leaves the slope free; the follower would start with a nonzero velocity, a velocity jump and an infinite acceleration spike at the start.
  3. For cams you often need continuous jerk too, which leads to quintic splines or B-splines of higher degree.

04.06.title: Numerical differentiation of noisy data
04.06.html:
A displacement sensor on a test rig gives you position every millisecond. You want velocity and acceleration. Differentiating the samples directly, with the finite differences from Phase 01, produces garbage: each difference divides a small noise by a small step. This lesson quantifies the problem and fixes it the way instrumentation engineers do, by fitting before differentiating.

Why noise explodes

Write each sample as xi​=x(ti​)+ηi​ with independent noise of standard deviation σ. The central difference gives

2hxi+1​−xi−1​​=x′(ti​)+truncation6h2​x′′′​​+noise2hηi+1​−ηi−1​​​​.

The noise term has standard deviation 2​σ/(2h)=σ/(2​h). Sampling faster makes it worse. A second derivative is worse again, scaling like σ/h2. At 1 kHz with 0.1 mm noise the velocity noise is about 0.07 m/s, and a raw second difference has about 245 m/s² of noise, 25 g.

Fit first: Savitzky-Golay

Around each sample take a window of 2m+1 points, fit a low-degree polynomial by least squares (Phase 02), and differentiate the polynomial at the centre. Because the fit is linear in the data, the whole operation is a fixed set of weights ck​, a convolution:

x^′(ti​)=k=−m∑m​ck​xi+k​.

For a quadratic (or linear) fit the first-derivative weights are simply ck​=k/(h∑k2), the least-squares slope. Their noise gain is σ/(h∑k2​), which falls like m−3/2. The price is bias: a wide window flattens fast features. Choose the window to span a small fraction of the shortest period you care about.

Worked exampleVelocity from a shaker test

Position x=0.05sin(2π⋅1.5t) m, sampled at h=1 ms with σ=0.1 mm noise. True peak speed 0.05⋅2π⋅1.5=0.471 m/s.

  1. Raw central difference: predicted noise σ/(2​h)=10−4/(1.414×10−3)=0.0707 m/s; measured RMS error 0.0718 m/s, 15% of the peak.
  2. Savitzky-Golay, 51-point window, quadratic: noise gain σ/(h2∑125​k2​)=10−4/(10−3⋅105.1)=0.00095 m/s.
  3. Measured RMS error 0.00213 m/s, which includes the small bias of fitting a parabola over 51 ms of a 667 ms period. Better than raw by a factor of 34.

  2. True peak acceleration 0.05(2π⋅1.5)2=4.44 m/s².
  3. The noise is 55 times the signal. You must smooth (a Savitzky-Golay second-derivative filter or a low-pass filter) or measure acceleration directly with an accelerometer.

04.07.title: Gaussian quadrature
04.07.html:
Every finite-element stiffness matrix, every mass matrix and every load vector is built from integrals over elements, evaluated millions of times. Each function evaluation costs. Gaussian quadrature answers a sharp question: with n evaluations, what is the most accurate rule possible? Answer: place the points at the roots of a Legendre polynomial and you integrate every polynomial up to degree 2n−1 exactly, twice what equally spaced points achieve.

Counting the freedom

A rule ∫−11​f(x)dx≈∑i=1n​wi​f(xi​) has 2n free numbers: n nodes and n weights. Demanding exactness for 1,x,x2,…,x2n−1 gives 2n equations. For n=2, symmetry gives x1,2​=±a, w1​=w2​=1 (from ∫1=2), and ∫x2=2/3 requires 2a2=2/3:

∫−11​fdx≈f(−3​1​)+f(3​1​),

exact for cubics. The three-point rule uses 0 and ±3/5​ with weights 8/9 and 5/9.

Why Legendre roots

Divide a polynomial f of degree ≤2n−1 by the Legendre polynomial Pn​: f=qPn​+r with q and r of degree ≤n−1. Legendre polynomials are orthogonal, so ∫qPn​=0. At the roots of Pn​, f(xi​)=r(xi​), and an n-point rule with the right weights is exact for the degree-(n−1) remainder r. So the rule is exact for f.

Computing nodes: Golub-Welsch

Legendre polynomials satisfy a three-term recurrence, which can be written as an eigenvalue problem. The nodes are the eigenvalues of the symmetric tridiagonal matrix with off-diagonal entries βk​=k/4k2−1​, and the weights are wi​=2v1,i2​ from the first components of the normalised eigenvectors. Phase 02’s eigenvalue machinery does the rest.

For an interval [a,b], map x=2b−a​t+2a+b​ and multiply the sum by 2b−a​.

Worked exampleTwo points, exact cubic

Integrate f(x)=x3+x2 on [0,2] with the two-point rule.

  1. Map: x=t+1, scale factor (b−a)/2=1. Nodes x=1∓0.57735: 0.42265 and 1.57735.
  2. f(0.42265)=0.25413 and f(1.57735)=6.41253.
  3. Sum: 6.66667. Exact: 424​+323​=4+2.66667=6.66667. Exact, as promised for a cubic.
  4. For ∫02​e−x2dx=0.882081, errors with 2 to 6 points are 3.7×10−2, 3.2×10−3, 1.5×10−4, 3.4×10−6, 3.5×10−8. Simpson with 5 points is still at 2.7×10−4.

04.08.title: Explicit Euler and stability
04.08.html:
A simulation that runs for a while and then shoots off to 10300 is the most common surprise in engineering computing. It is rarely a bug in the physics. It is the time step violating the stability limit of the integrator. You can predict that limit exactly with one line of algebra, and this lesson shows how.

The test equation

Linearise any system around an operating point and diagonalise it: each mode behaves like

y′=λy,y(0)=1,y(t)=eλt,

with λ an eigenvalue of the Jacobian (Phase 02). Real negative λ is a decaying mode (cooling, damping); complex λ with negative real part is a damped oscillation.

One step of Euler

Explicit Euler, yn+1​=yn​+hf(yn​), applied to the test equation gives

yn+1​=(1+hλ)yn​⟹yn​=(1+hλ)n.

The numerical solution decays only if the amplification factor satisfies ∣1+hλ∣≤1. In the complex z=hλ plane that is a disc of radius 1 centred at −1: the stability region. For a real decay rate λ=−k:

∣1−hk∣≤1⟺h≤k2​.

For 1/k<h<2/k the solution still decays but flips sign every step: stable, but qualitatively wrong. Purely imaginary λ (an undamped oscillator) is never inside the disc: Euler always adds energy to a spring-mass system.

Stiffness

For a system, every mode must be stable, so the fastest mode sets the step, even after it has decayed to nothing. Eigenvalues −1 and −1000 force h<0.002 s, so 5000 steps to cover 10 s of a slow transient. That is a stiff system, and lesson 04.11 cures it with implicit methods.

Worked exampleA thermocouple bead

A bead with time constant τ=0.5 s obeys y′=−2y (k=2 s⁻¹). Integrate with explicit Euler for 50 steps.

1.0 −1 1, oscillating forever
1.1 −1.2 9.1×103, blown up

The boundary is exactly h=2/k=1 s, and the code checks it at 59 step sizes.

04.09.title: Runge-Kutta methods
04.09.html:
Euler’s method looks at the slope once per step and walks in a straight line. Runge-Kutta methods sample the slope several times inside the step and combine the samples so that the errors cancel up to a high power of h. Classical RK4 needs four slope evaluations per step and is fourth order: halve the step and the error drops 16 times. It’s been the workhorse for well-behaved ODEs for over a century.

Deriving RK2 by matching Taylor series

Propose a two-stage method for y′=f(t,y):

k1​=f(tn​,yn​),k2​=f(tn​+c2​h, yn​+a21​hk1​),yn+1​=yn​+h(b1​k1​+b2​k2​).

Expand k2​ to first order: k2​≈f+c2​hft​+a21​hffy​. The exact solution has y(t+h)=y+hf+2h2​(ft​+ffy​)+O(h3). Matching terms:

b1​+b2​=1,b2​c2​=21​,b2​a21​=21​.

One free parameter. b2​=21​ gives Heun’s method (c2​=1); b2​=1 gives the midpoint method (c2​=21​). Both have local error O(h3) and global error O(h2).

Butcher tableaus

Any explicit RK method is a table of coefficients: ci​ (stage times), aij​ (how stages combine) and bi​ (final weights). Classical RK4:

021​21​1​21​0061​​21​031​​131​​61​​​

One engine that reads a tableau can run every method, which is how libraries are written. The code below does exactly that.

Is more stages always better?

Cost is counted in function evaluations. To reach error 10−6 on a smooth problem, RK4 typically needs far fewer evaluations than Euler: in the example below, RK4 with 200 evaluations beats Euler with 20 000 by more than two orders of magnitude. For non-smooth problems (impacts, friction switching) the high order is wasted at the discontinuities, which is one reason adaptive methods (next lesson) exist.

04.10.title: Adaptive step size
04.10.html:
A ball dropped on a hard floor spends almost a second in smooth free flight and under two milliseconds in contact, where the forces are thousands of times larger. A fixed step small enough for the contact wastes thousands of steps in flight; a step sized for the flight jumps straight through the floor. Adaptive integrators measure their own error every step and adjust h to meet a tolerance you set. They’re the default in every serious ODE library.

Estimating the error for free

Run two methods of different order from the same point and compare. An embedded pair shares all its stage evaluations: the Dormand-Prince pair computes seven stages, combines them one way for a fifth-order result y(5) and another way for a fourth-order y(4). Their difference estimates the local error of the lower-order one:

err=​atol+rtol∣y∣y(5)−y(4)​​RMS​.

Scaling by atol+rtol∣y∣ makes err≤1 mean “within tolerance”. The method then carries on with the fifth-order value (local extrapolation), and since the seventh stage equals the first stage of the next step, each accepted step costs six new evaluations.

Choosing the next step

Local error of a fourth-order estimate scales like h5, so to hit err=1:

hnew​=h⋅min(5, max(0.2, 0.9err−1/5)).

If err>1 the step is rejected and retried with the smaller h. The safety factor 0.9 and the limits 0.2 and 5 stop the controller from oscillating.

Local tolerance, global error

The controller bounds the error made in each step, not the accumulated error at the end. For well-behaved problems the global error ends up close to the tolerance, which the code checks; for chaotic or unstable problems it can be much larger. Always repeat a run at a tighter tolerance and compare: if the answer changes, it wasn’t converged.

Large steps also mean the solution is only known at a few points. To plot it, or to find the apex of a bounce, use dense output: an interpolant built from the stage values. The widget below uses a cubic Hermite curve through the position and velocity at each accepted step, which is exact for a free-flight parabola.

04.11.title: Stiff equations and implicit methods
04.11.html:
A rubber bushing, a contact spring, a fast chemical reaction or a stiff structural mode settles in milliseconds, while the motion you care about lasts seconds. Explicit methods must resolve the fastest mode forever, even after it has died away. Implicit methods evaluate the slope at the end of the step instead of the start. Each step needs an equation solve, but the step can be as large as accuracy allows, often thousands of times larger.

Backward Euler

yn+1​=yn​+hf(tn+1​,yn+1​).

The unknown appears on both sides. On the test equation y′=λy:

yn+1​=1−hλyn​​,R(z)=1−z1​.

∣R(z)∣≤1 for every z with Rez≤0: the method is A-stable. For y′=−ky at h=100/k the amplification is 1/101, a perfectly tame decay, where explicit Euler’s factor would be −99. As z→−∞, R→0: fast modes are damped out at once. That property, L-stability, is exactly what you want for stiff transients.

Newton inside every step

For a nonlinear f, each step solves G(z)=z−yn​−hf(z)=0 with Newton’s method (lesson 04.03):

(I−hJ)Δz=−G(z),J=∂y∂f​.

Start from z=yn​; a few iterations suffice because the guess is close. Production codes reuse one factorisation of I−hJ for several steps.

Stable is not accurate

Backward Euler is only first order. Large steps give a stable, smooth answer that may miss the fast transient entirely, which is fine if you only care about the slow motion. For accuracy, use higher-order implicit methods: BDF formulas (SciPy BDF) or implicit Runge-Kutta (Radau). The trapezoidal rule (Crank-Nicolson, lesson 04.14) is second order and A-stable but not L-stable, so very fast modes ring instead of dying.

Worked exampleA stiff bushing

mx¨+cx˙+kx(1+(x/d)2)=F with m=0.01 kg, c=20 N s/m, k=104 N/m, d=1 mm, F=10 N, starting at rest.

  1. Linearised at rest: λ2+2000λ+106=0, so λ=−1000 s⁻¹ twice (critically damped). Explicit Euler needs h<2/1000=2 ms.
  2. Static deflection: with s=x/d, s+s3=1 gives s=0.6823, so x=0.6823 mm.
  3. Backward Euler with h=0.1 s (h∣λ∣=100): after 2 s, x=0.6823 mm, with 1 to 6 Newton iterations per step.
  4. Explicit Euler with the same step: ∣x∣=2×103 m after 3 steps.
  5. Accuracy of the transient at t=2 ms: error 14.70 µm at h=100 µs and 7.47 µm at h=50 µs. Halving h halves the error: first order.

04.12.title: Symplectic integrators
04.12.html:
Simulate a satellite for a year, a molecular dynamics run for a billion steps, or a pendulum clock for a week, and a new kind of error dominates: slow drift in energy. RK4 is extremely accurate per step, yet its energy error grows steadily, without bound. Symplectic integrators such as velocity Verlet make a larger error per step but never drift: the energy error oscillates within a fixed band forever. For long runs of conservative systems, that’s the property that matters.

Hamiltonian structure

A frictionless mechanical system has position q, momentum p and energy H(q,p)=T(p)+V(q), with

q˙​=∂p∂H​,p˙​=−∂q∂H​.

The exact flow conserves H and also preserves phase-space area (Liouville’s theorem). Explicit Euler expands area (its spirals go outward, gaining energy), RK4 shrinks it slightly. A symplectic method preserves area exactly. A deep result (backward error analysis) says it then exactly conserves a slightly modified energy H~=H+O(h2), so the true energy can only wobble, not drift.

Velocity Verlet

For q¨​=a(q):

vn+1/2​=vn​+2h​a(qn​),qn+1​=qn​+hvn+1/2​,vn+1​=vn+1/2​+2h​a(qn+1​).

Second order, symplectic, time-reversible, and only one force evaluation per step (the last one is reused at the next step). It is the standard in molecular dynamics, orbital mechanics and game physics. Its cousin, symplectic Euler (update v first, then q with the new v), is first order but also has bounded energy error.

Worked exampleTen times longer, same error

A pendulum (L=1 m) released from 60°, step h=0.05 s:

run Verlet: worst energy error RK4: energy error at end
10 000 steps (500 s) 5.62×10−3 1.43×10−3
100 000 steps (5000 s) 5.62×10−3 1.43×10−2

RK4’s error grows tenfold with a tenfold longer run; Verlet’s worst error does not move. Now compare at equal cost: RK4 uses four force evaluations per step, so give it h=0.2 s for the same budget. After 5000 s it has lost essentially all of the pendulum’s energy (relative error 1.00). The same code keeps an eccentric (e=0.5) Kepler orbit within 2.7×10−4 relative energy error over 159 orbits.

04.13.title: Finite differences in 1D
04.13.html:
So far you’ve integrated in time. Many engineering problems are boundary-value problems in space instead: the temperature along a heated rod, the deflection of a cable, the pressure along a pipe. Finite differences replace derivatives by differences on a grid and turn the differential equation into a linear system. It is the simplest discretisation there is, and everything about it (stencils, matrices, boundary conditions, convergence) carries over to the 2D and 3D solvers that follow.

Stencils from Taylor series

Expand u(x±h):

u(x±h)=u±hu′+2h2​u′′±6h3​u′′′+24h4​u′′′′+…

Add the two and the odd terms cancel:

u′′(x)=h2u(x−h)−2u(x)+u(x+h)​−12h2​u′′′′(ξ).

Second order. The stencil is exact whenever u′′′′=0, so for any cubic.

From equation to matrix

For −u′′=f on [0,L] with u(0)=ua​ and u(L)=ub​, put n cells of width h=L/n and write the stencil at each interior node i=1,…,n−1:

h21​​2−1​−12⋱​−1⋱−1​⋱2​​​u1​u2​⋮un−1​​​=​f1​+ua​/h2f2​⋮fn−1​+ub​/h2​​.

Known boundary values move to the right-hand side. The matrix is tridiagonal, symmetric and positive definite, with eigenvalues h24​sin22Lkπh​. The smallest approximates (π/L)2, the continuous eigenvalue; the largest is about 4/h2. Their ratio, the condition number, grows like 1/h2, which matters for iterative solvers (lesson 04.17).

A prescribed flux u′(0)=g (a Neumann condition, Phase 03) needs a ghost node u−1​=u1​−2hg to stay second order.

Worked exampleA rod heated by an electric current

A 100 mm steel rod (k=50 W/(m K)) generates q=1 MW/m³ and both ends are held at 20 °C. Steady conduction: −kT′′=q.

  1. Exact solution: T=20+2kq​x(L−x), with centre value 20+8kqL2​=20+400106⋅0.01​=45 °C.
  2. Finite differences with only 10 cells give 45.0000 °C at the centre, exact to rounding at every node, because the solution is quadratic and the stencil is exact for polynomials up to degree 3.
  3. For a solution that isn’t a polynomial, −u′′=π2sinπx: max errors 8.27×10−3, 2.06×10−3, 5.14×10−4, 1.29×10−4 for 10, 20, 40, 80 cells. Observed orders 2.005, 2.001, 2.000.

04.14.title: Heat equation, explicit and implicit
04.14.html:
Lesson 03.14 solved the cooling of a rod with a Fourier series. Real parts have awkward shapes, varying properties and time-dependent boundaries, so you need a time-stepping solver. Discretise space with the stencil from the last lesson and time with Euler or the trapezoidal rule, and you get the two classic schemes: FTCS, simple but bound by a strict time-step limit, and Crank-Nicolson, implicit and stable at any step.

FTCS: forward time, centred space

For ut​=αuxx​ on a grid xi​=iΔx, tn​=nΔt:

uin+1​=uin​+r(ui+1n​−2uin​+ui−1n​),r=Δx2αΔt​.

Each new value is a weighted average of three old ones, with weights r, 1−2r, r. If r>1/2 the centre weight goes negative and the scheme overshoots.

Von Neumann stability analysis

Insert a single Fourier mode uin​=GneikiΔx:

G=1−4rsin22kΔx​.

The worst mode is the grid-scale zig-zag (kΔx=π), with G=1−4r. Requiring ∣G∣≤1 gives

r≤21​⟺Δt≤2αΔx2​.

Halving Δx forces a quarter of the time step: four times the steps on twice the nodes, eight times the work. That is why explicit heat solvers get expensive on fine grids.

Crank-Nicolson

Average the spatial operator between the old and new time levels (the trapezoidal rule in time):

(I+2r​A)un+1=(I−2r​A)un,A=tridiag(−1,2,−1).

One tridiagonal solve per step, O(n). The amplification factor is

G=1+2rsin2(kΔx/2)1−2rsin2(kΔx/2)​,

always between −1 and 1: unconditionally stable and second order in both time and space. At large r, G→−1 for the zig-zag mode, so sharp initial corners ring for a few steps before decaying. Starting with a couple of backward Euler steps removes that.

Worked exampleCooling an aluminium rod

04.15.title: Wave equation and CFL
04.15.html:
A plucked guitar string, a pressure pulse in a hydraulic line, a stress wave in a bar after an impact: all obey the wave equation utt​=c2uxx​. Information travels at speed c, and a numerical scheme must respect that. The CFL condition (Courant, Friedrichs and Lewy, 1928) says the numerical domain of dependence must contain the physical one. Break it and the solution explodes; meet it exactly and, for this equation, the scheme is exact.

Leapfrog

Centred differences in both time and space:

uin+1​=2uin​−uin−1​+σ2(ui+1n​−2uin​+ui−1n​),σ=ΔxcΔt​.

σ is the Courant number. Starting from rest, the first step uses ui1​=ui0​+2σ2​(ui+10​−2ui0​+ui−10​).

The CFL condition

In one step, the scheme only lets information move one cell, a distance Δx. The physical wave moves cΔt. If cΔt>Δx, the true solution at a node depends on data the scheme never sees, and it cannot converge. Von Neumann analysis makes it precise:

sin2ωΔt​=σsin2kΔx​,

which has real frequencies for every mode only if σ≤1. Above 1, the grid-scale mode grows exponentially.

At σ=1 exactly, ω=ck for every mode: no dispersion, and leapfrog reproduces d’Alembert’s solution exactly at the nodes. Below 1, short waves travel slightly too slowly (numerical dispersion), so sharp kinks smear into ripples.

Worked exampleA guitar’s high E string

Scale length L=648 mm, fundamental f1​=329.63 Hz, plucked 2 mm high at 20% of the length.

  1. Wave speed c=2Lf1​=2⋅0.648⋅329.63=427.2 m/s; period 1/f1​=3.0337 ms.
  2. With 100 cells, Δx=6.48 mm and the CFL limit is Δt≤Δx/c=15.17 µs: 200 steps per period.
  3. After exactly one period the string should be back in its plucked shape. Measured maximum deviation: 2.8×10−15 mm at CFL 1.000 (exact), 0.089 mm at CFL 0.5 (4% of the amplitude, from dispersion), and 5×1030 mm at CFL 1.02.

  1. Δx=300/600=0.5 m.
  2. Δt≤Δx/c=0.5/1200=0.417 ms.
  3. 2/0.000417=4800 steps. At CFL exactly 1 the scheme is also dispersion-free, so a standard choice in water hammer codes (the method of characteristics) is to run at σ=1.

04.16.title: Advection and upwinding
04.16.html:
A slug of dye released into a river, heat carried by coolant through a pipe, smoke in a ventilation duct: quantities that are carried by a flow obey the advection equation. It looks like the simplest PDE there is, yet it breaks naive schemes in instructive ways. The fix, upwinding (taking information from the direction the flow comes from), is the foundation of every CFD code in Phase 17.

The advection equation

For a concentration q(x,t) carried at speed U>0:

qt​+Uqx​=0,q(x,t)=q0​(x−Ut).

The profile slides downstream unchanged. A good scheme should move it at the right speed, keep it positive and not invent new peaks.

Three schemes

With c=UΔt/Δx:

  • Central (FTCS): qin+1​=qin​−2c​(qi+1n​−qi−1n​). Von Neumann gives ∣G∣2=1+c2sin2θ>1: unstable for every c. Don’t use it.
  • Upwind: qin+1​=qin​−c(qin​−qi−1n​), using the upstream neighbour. Stable for c≤1, and each new value is a convex combination (1−c)qi​+cqi−1​ of old ones, so it is monotone: no new maxima, no negative concentrations.
  • Lax-Wendroff: adds the term 2c2​(qi+1​−2qi​+qi−1​) to the central scheme, making it stable and second order, but not monotone.

The modified equation

Expand the upwind scheme in Taylor series and ask which PDE it actually solves to the next order:

qt​+Uqx​=Dnum​qxx​,Dnum​=2UΔx​(1−c).

Upwind solves advection plus a numerical diffusion. It smears sharp fronts, more so on coarse grids and at small CFL numbers, and it’s exact at c=1. Godunov’s theorem says no linear scheme can be both monotone and better than first order; modern codes beat it with nonlinear flux limiters that switch between upwind near fronts and second order elsewhere.

Worked exampleDye in a river

River speed U=0.5 m/s, a 100 m slug at concentration 1 centred at x=300 m, cells of Δx=5 m, CFL c=0.8, run for 2000 s (the slug travels 1000 m).

scheme max min total mass
upwind 0.886 0 100.00
Lax-Wendroff 1.194 −0.192 100.00
central 2.6×1025 −2.6×1025 blown up

Upwind’s centre of mass is at exactly 1300 m. The modified equation predicts Dnum​=0.5⋅5⋅0.2/2=0.25 m²/s, so the pulse variance should grow from 1002/12=833 m² to 833+2Dnum​t=1833 m². Measured: 1831 m².

Exercise 1Is the smearing physical?

The river’s real turbulent dispersion coefficient is about 5 m²/s. With Δx=20 m and c=0.5, how does upwind’s numerical diffusion compare?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Dnum​=2UΔx​(1−c)=20.5⋅20​⋅0.5=2.5 m²/s.
  2. That’s half the physical value: the model would overstate the spreading by 50%. The numerical error is the same size as the physics.
  3. Fixes: refine to Δx=2 m (Dnum​=0.25 m²/s, 5% of physical), run closer to c=1, or use a second-order limited scheme.

04.17.title: 2D Poisson solvers
04.17.html:
Steady temperature in a plate, the stress function in a twisted shaft, pressure in incompressible flow, electrostatic potential: all are Poisson problems −∇2u=f. Lesson 03.16 solved one with SOR without saying much about why it works or how to choose its parameter. This lesson builds the three classic iterations, explains their speed through eigenvalues, and shows that the right relaxation factor turns thousands of iterations into about a hundred.

The 5-point system

On an n×n grid with spacing h,

h24ui,j​−ui+1,j​−ui−1,j​−ui,j+1​−ui,j−1​​=fi,j​.

That’s (n−1)2 unknowns with a sparse, symmetric positive definite matrix. Direct sparse solvers work well in 2D; iterative methods matter for very large or 3D problems, and they’re the stepping stone to multigrid.

Three iterations

  • Jacobi: replace every value by the average of its four neighbours plus h2f/4, using only old values.
  • Gauss-Seidel: the same, but use new values as soon as they are computed. About twice as fast as Jacobi.
  • SOR: compute the Gauss-Seidel value and overshoot it: u←(1−ω)u+ωuGS​ with 1<ω<2.

Why they’re slow, and how fast SOR can be

The error shrinks each iteration by the spectral radius ρ of the iteration matrix. For the model problem:

ρJ​=cosπh,ρGS​=cos2πh,ωopt​=1+sinπh2​,ρSOR​=ωopt​−1.

For small h, Jacobi has ρ≈1−π2h2/2: the number of iterations grows like 1/h2, so like n2. With ωopt​, SOR has ρ≈1−2πh, so iterations grow only like n. The slow components are always the smooth, long-wavelength errors, which local averaging barely touches. That observation leads straight to multigrid in the next lesson.

Worked exampleA 32 × 32 plate

−∇2u=2π2sinπxsinπy on the unit square with u=0 on the edges (exact u=sinπxsinπy), n=32, iterating until the residual falls by 108.

  1. ωopt​=2/(1+sin(π/32))=1.8215.
  2. Iterations: Jacobi 3817, Gauss-Seidel 1945, SOR 126. SOR is 15 times faster than Gauss-Seidel and 30 times faster than Jacobi.
  3. Prediction for Jacobi: ln10−8/lncos(π/32)=3816 iterations. The right-hand side is a single eigenmode, so the prediction is essentially exact.
  4. All three reach the same discretisation error, 8.04×10−4: iterating further can’t beat the grid.

Exercise 1Doubling the grid

Estimate the iteration counts for Jacobi and optimal SOR at n=64, from the n=32 results.

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Jacobi iterations scale like 1/h2: 3817⋅4≈15300. Check: ln10−8/lncos(π/64)=15283.
  2. SOR scales like 1/h: about 126⋅2≈250.
  3. Each iteration also costs four times as much on the finer grid, so Jacobi’s total work grows 16 times, SOR’s 8 times. Multigrid’s grows only 4 times, in proportion to the unknowns.

04.18.title: Multigrid intuition
04.18.html:
The last lesson ended with a frustration: simple iterations kill jagged errors quickly but crawl on smooth ones, so their cost explodes as the grid is refined. Multigrid turns that weakness into a strategy. A smooth error on a fine grid looks jagged on a coarser grid, where the same simple iteration kills it cheaply. Cycle between grids and the cost of a solve becomes proportional to the number of unknowns, the best possible. Modern FE and CFD codes rely on it, often hidden inside an “algebraic multigrid” preconditioner.

Smoothers smooth

Weighted Jacobi with ω=2/3 on −u′′=f multiplies the error mode sin(kπx) by

g(k)=1−2ωsin22kπh​.

For the upper half of the modes (kh≥1/2), ∣g∣≤1/3: each sweep removes at least two thirds of every rough component, whatever the grid size. For the smoothest mode g≈1−ωπ2h2/2, almost 1. So after a few sweeps the error is smooth, not small. That’s why the method is called a smoother.

Coarse-grid correction

A smooth error can be represented on a grid with half the points. The two-grid cycle:

  1. Pre-smooth: a few weighted-Jacobi sweeps on the fine grid.
  2. Restrict the residual r=f−Au to the coarse grid with full weighting (41​,21​,41​).
  3. Solve the coarse error equation A2h​e2h​=r2h​.
  4. Prolong e2h​ back by linear interpolation and correct: u←u+Pe2h​.
  5. Post-smooth to remove the jaggedness that the interpolation introduces.

Solve step 3 the same way, recursively, and you have a V-cycle. The work per cycle is about twice that of one fine-grid sweep (the grids sum to n+n/2+n/4+⋯≈2n), and the error reduction per cycle is independent of n.

Worked exampleGrid-independent convergence

−u′′=f on [0,1] with a random right-hand side (all frequencies present), two pre- and two post-smoothing sweeps. Average residual reduction per cycle:

n two-grid V-cycle
32 0.050 0.085
64 0.057 0.087
128 0.057 0.086
256 0.058 0.086
512 0.058 0.086
1024 0.058 0.086

Each V-cycle gains more than a digit, at every size. Eight cycles reach about 10−8 whether the grid has 32 or 1024 cells; Jacobi would need about 103 times more sweeps on the finest grid than on the coarsest.

Exercise 1Cost of a V-cycle in 2D

In 2D each coarser grid has a quarter of the points. If one smoothing sweep on the finest grid costs 1 unit and the V-cycle does 4 sweeps per level, what does a V-cycle cost?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. Levels cost 4(1+41​+161​+…)=4⋅1−1/41​=5.33 units.
  2. That’s only a third more than the 4 sweeps on the finest grid alone.
  3. With a reduction factor near 0.1 per cycle, reaching 10−8 takes about 8 cycles, about 43 sweep-equivalents, at any grid size.

04.19.title: Optimisation algorithms
04.19.html:
Lighter brackets, stiffer frames, cheaper pipe networks, controllers that settle faster: design is optimisation. Phase 02 solved least squares, the one optimisation problem with a closed-form answer. Most design problems need iterative methods that walk downhill on an objective function. This lesson builds the two you’ll meet most: gradient descent, which is simple but slow on badly scaled problems, and BFGS, the quasi-Newton workhorse behind scipy.optimize.minimize.

Gradient descent and line search

Step against the gradient, xk+1​=xk​−αk​∇f(xk​). A fixed step is either too timid or unstable. A backtracking line search starts from α=1 and halves it until the Armijo condition holds:

f(x+αp)≤f(x)+c1​α∇fTp,c1​=10−4.

This guarantees a real decrease. But in a long, narrow valley the gradient points mostly across the valley, not along it, so the iterates zig-zag. The number of iterations grows with the condition number of the Hessian (lesson 03.03).

Newton and quasi-Newton

Newton’s method for optimisation uses the Hessian: solve Hp=−∇f. It rescales the problem so every valley looks round, and converges quadratically near the minimum. But Hessians are expensive or unavailable. BFGS builds an approximation of H−1 from the gradients it has already seen. With s=xk+1​−xk​, y=∇fk+1​−∇fk​ and ρ=1/(yTs):

Hk+1−1​=(I−ρsyT)Hk−1​(I−ρysT)+ρssT.

The update satisfies the secant condition Hk+1−1​y=s (the multidimensional version of the secant method from 04.02) and stays positive definite as long as yTs>0. Convergence is superlinear, and each iteration needs only one gradient.

The Rosenbrock valley

f(x1​,x2​)=(1−x1​)2+100(x2​−x12​)2 has its minimum at (1,1), at the end of a curved, banana-shaped valley. It’s the standard torture test for optimisers.

Worked exampleRosenbrock from (−1.2,1)

Both methods use the same Armijo backtracking and stop when ∥∇f∥<10−10.

  1. BFGS: reaches (1.00000000,1.00000000) in 36 iterations. SciPy’s BFGS (with a stronger Wolfe line search) needs 32.
  2. Gradient descent: 25 115 iterations to the same tolerance, about 700 times more.
  3. Why: at the minimum the Hessian is (802−400​−400200​), with condition number about 2500. Steepest descent pays for that ratio; BFGS learns it.

Exercise 1One Armijo backtrack

At x=(−1.2,1), f=24.2 and ∇f=(−215.6,−88). Taking p=−∇f, does the full step α=1 satisfy Armijo? Roughly what step will be accepted?

Show step-by-step solution
  1. ∇fTp=−(215.62+882)=−54227. The full step lands at (214.4,89), where f is about 2×1011. Armijo fails badly.
  2. Halving repeatedly, Armijo first holds after 10 halvings: α=2−10≈0.001, a move of (0.21,0.09). The step had to shrink to the width of the valley.
  3. This is why scaling matters: one badly scaled direction forces tiny steps in all of them. BFGS’s H−1 fixes the scaling after a few iterations.

04.20.title: Verification and validation
04.20.html:
A simulation produces beautiful colour plots whether it is right or not. Before anyone builds a part on the strength of your results, two questions must have documented answers. Verification: are we solving the equations right? (Is the code a correct implementation of the model?) Validation: are we solving the right equations? (Does the model match reality?) This lesson gives you the sharpest verification tool there is, the method of manufactured solutions, and closes Phase 04 by turning everything you have built into something you can trust.

Code verification by observed order

Every discretisation in this phase has a theoretical order p. If the code is correct, refining the grid must make the error fall like hp. The test needs an exact solution to measure the error against, and real problems rarely have one.

The method of manufactured solutions

Turn the problem around: choose the solution first, then compute what source term and boundary data produce it.

  1. Pick a smooth um​(x,y) that exercises every term: not a polynomial the scheme reproduces exactly, not a single eigenmode, with nonzero boundary values. For example um​=sin(πx)ey+xy2.
  2. Derive the source by applying the operator by hand (or with computer algebra): f=−∇2um​=(π2−1)sin(πx)ey−2x.
  3. Run the solver with that f and boundary values um​ on a sequence of grids.
  4. Measure the error and the observed order pobs​=log2​(Eh​/Eh/2​). Pass if it approaches the theoretical order.

The manufactured solution needn’t be physical. It’s a test pattern, and a far stricter test than “the plot looks plausible”: a bug that adds an O(h) error passes every eyeball check and fails MMS immediately.

Solution verification and validation

  • Solution verification estimates the discretisation error of a real run, where no exact solution exists: compute on three grids, check that the observed order is near theory, and extrapolate (Richardson, lesson 04.01). Report the estimated uncertainty, not just the answer.
  • Validation compares the verified model with experiments, with uncertainties on both sides. A mismatch then points at the physics (material model, boundary conditions, turbulence model), not at the code.

Only verified codes can be meaningfully validated. Calibrating a buggy code to match an experiment just hides the bug until the next design.

Worked exampleCatching a planted bug

The 5-point Poisson solver on the unit square with um​=sin(πx)ey+xy2 (maximum value 3.22):

n 8 16 32 64 128
correct: max error 1.32×10−2 3.34×10−3 8.36×10−4 2.09×10−4 5.23×10−5
bug: max error 1.65×10−1 9.41×10−2 5.02×10−2 2.59×10−2 1.32×10−2

Observed orders: correct 1.98, 2.00, 2.00, 2.00; buggy 0.81, 0.91, 0.95, 0.98. The buggy solver’s error at n=128 is only 0.4% of the solution, and its contour plots are indistinguishable by eye. Only the order gives it away.

Exercise 1Manufacture a source term

For the 1D heat equation ut​=αuxx​+s(x,t), manufacture um​=e−tsin(2x)+x2. What source s must you add, and what boundary data at x=0 and x=π?

  2. s=ut​−αuxx​=−e−tsin2x+4αe−tsin2x−2α=(4α−1)e−tsin2x−2α.
  3. Boundary values: u(0,t)=0 and u(π,t)=π2; initial condition u(x,0)=sin2x+x2. Run FTCS and Crank-Nicolson (04.14) with this s: the observed orders in time should be 1 and 2.
